prompt:
Use the attached image as the reference: the same woman — the personification of Argon (Ar) — seen off duty in her everyday life. Keep her face, eye colour, hair colour, skin tone and body exactly; change only her clothes, pose and place. Do not reuse earlier conversation images.

Behind her, a richly painted background with layered painterly colour, subtle visible brushwork, atmospheric perspective and cinematic depth. Luminous, rich colours; crisp focal details on the face and costume, softer painted edges toward the distance. No flat single-tone cel shading, photographic appearance, semi-realistic face or plastic 3D-render finish. Keep this rendering exactly as in the attached image — the same finish, line, shading, skin and colour treatment.

COMPOSITION: an environmental long shot, her complete figure and enough of the place around her; body in side profile, her face in profile too, not turned toward the camera, facing the right of the frame, so her own right side is toward the camera; camera slightly above, looking down at her; she is placed in the left third of the frame, open space of the place to her right; the space runs far back behind her, its lines receding into the distance.
Lens / perspective: 35mm-equivalent environmental perspective balancing the woman and the setting with moderate depth.
RIGHT HAND: her own right hand rests on her knee — her near arm, on the camera side.
LEFT HAND: her own left hand is planted on the ground beside her — her far arm, on the side away from the camera.
LEGS: legs folded cross-legged.
GAZE: she looks toward the far distance.
EXPRESSION: one mouth corner lifted higher than the other, lips closed.
Scene note: she is the orchard keeper who would rather nap than pick

Leave behind everything she wears in the attached image — no crown, tiara, helmet, feathers, headpiece, hairpins from it, armour or regalia; her hair is styled for the everyday outfit, with at most one small accessory.

Her element — argon: 'the lazy one', a noble gas that reacts with nothing, yet makes up nearly one percent of the air — more than all the other noble gases together; found in 1894 by Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay because nitrogen taken from air weighed a little more than nitrogen made from chemicals, a stubborn residue Henry Cavendish had already noticed in 1785; glows soft lavender-violet in a discharge tube; a heavy, idle blanket laid over welding arcs, sealed inside light bulbs to keep their filaments alive, and over precious old documents to stop time; drowsy, gentle, protective — may show in the outfit's details, motifs or small accessories.
